Dip
DIP
v.t.
From Anglo-Saxon dyppan, to plunge into a liquid and withdraw. Webster 1828: to plunge or immerse for a moment in a liquid. In the Levitical system it is a priestly action word: the finger, the hyssop, the bird, all dipped in blood or water before anything is applied.

Biblical Definition

Nothing in the sanctuary was applied dry. The priest must first dip, and what he dips into is blood: the priest shall dip his finger in the blood, and sprinkle of the blood seven times before the LORD, before the vail of the sanctuary (Leviticus 4:6). The order is fixed and it is doctrine — contact with the blood precedes every application of it. Israel’s deliverance began the same way, with a bunch of hyssop: ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts (Exodus 12:22). The blood in the basin saved no one; the blood applied to the door did. Naaman learned the lesson against his pride: then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean (2 Kings 5:14) — cleansing by an appointed means, in an unimpressive river, at a prophet’s bare word. And John sees the King return with the action already accomplished on Himself: he was clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God (Revelation 19:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DIP as to plunge or immerse for a moment or short time in water or other liquid substance; to take by dipping; to wet, as with a liquid.

expand to see more

DIP, v.t. — To plunge or immerse, for a moment or short time, in water or other liquid substance.

To take with a ladle or other vessel by immersing it in a fluid; as, to dip water from a boiler.

To engage as a pledge; to take a concern in.

DIP, v.i. — To sink; to enter; to incline downward.

Anglo-Saxon dyppan, to dip; related to deep and to baptize in its plain sense of plunging.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 4:6 — "And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood, and sprinkle of the blood seven times before the LORD, before the vail of the sanctuary."

Exodus 12:22 — "And ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts with the blood that is in the bason; and none of you shall go out at the door of his house until the morning."

2 Kings 5:14 — "Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean."

Revelation 19:13 — "And he was clothed with a vesture dipped in blood: and his name is called The Word of God."

Modern Corruption

The plain sense of dipping — plunging and withdrawing — is the sense of the New Testament word for baptism, and every argument for sprinkling as the mode has to work against the vocabulary rather than with it.

expand to see more

Dip is the ordinary English for what bapto and baptizo describe, and Naaman in Jordan is the Old Testament picture the New Testament vocabulary reaches for. This dictionary holds believer’s baptism by immersion as the New Testament pattern, and the lexical point is a large part of the reason: the Greek word means to plunge, and every attempt to make it mean an application of a few drops must be argued around the word rather than from it. The 1689 Confession states it directly — immersion, the dipping of the person in water, is necessary to the due administration of the ordinance. Note also who is dipped: Naaman went down himself, at the word of God, having first been offended that the means were so plain. That is the order of faith, and infant baptism cannot reproduce it.

There is a second corruption to name, subtler and more common among the orthodox: treating the blood of Christ as sufficient in the basin. Exodus 12 is emphatic that the blood in the bason saved nobody in Egypt; the blood on the lintel did. The Reformed doctrine of the application of redemption — effectual calling, union with Christ, justification by faith — is exactly this insistence that what Christ purchased must be applied by the Spirit to the individual soul. A general atonement floating unapplied over mankind is a bason of blood and an unmarked door. Definite atonement says the Lamb was slain for His people and the blood is certainly struck on every door He purchased.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tabal (H2881), to dip, to immerse; Greek bapto (G911), to dip, to dye by dipping; baptizo (G907), to immerse, to submerge.

expand to see more

Hebrew tabal (H2881) — to dip or plunge; used of the priest’s finger (Leviticus 4:6), the hyssop (Exodus 12:22), and Naaman in Jordan (2 Kings 5:14).

Greek bapto (G911) — to dip, and so to dye by dipping; used of the vesture dipped in blood (Revelation 19:13).

Greek baptizo (G907) — the intensive form, to immerse or submerge; the New Testament word for the ordinance.

Hebrew ezob (H231) — hyssop, the bunch used to carry the blood from bason to lintel (Exodus 12:22).

Hebrew nazah (H5137) — to sprinkle, the action that follows the dipping (Leviticus 4:6).

Usage

"The priest shall dip his finger in the blood (Leviticus 4:6) — contact with the blood precedes every application of it."

"Dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel (Exodus 12:22) — the blood in the basin saved no one; the blood applied did."

"He dipped himself seven times in Jordan (2 Kings 5:14) — cleansing by an appointed means, at a prophet’s bare word."
